raw_response:
I'm 74 this year, and these old legs don't move like they used to. I've been growing cotton on these same 2 mu for fifty-five years — longer than most folks in the village have been alive. My son and his wife work over at the factory in town, so it's mostly me and my old man at home now. The children come back to help at harvest, thank goodness, because I can't bend down all day like I once could.

Two mu is not much land, but it's what we have, and I know every corner of it. I grow cotton because I understand it, and anyway the cotton buyer drives his truck right into the village come autumn, so I don't have to carry anything far. I plant around the third week of April, when the soil feels warm under your hand. This year I'm planting now, same as always — no point changing what works. I use the improved seed from the shop in town, about one packet per mu. Costs a bit, but saved seed doesn't grow as strong anymore.

For fertilizer, I don't have money to waste. I bought one big bag of compound fertilizer — the kind with the three kinds in it — and I spread half a bag's worth on each mu before planting, then work it into the soil. When the cotton starts flowering in July, if it looks hungry I'll topdress with a little urea, maybe a quarter bag per mu. Old Wang down the road puts on more, but he has ten mu and his son sends money home. I can't afford to throw away cash on fertilizer that might just wash away.

Water costs money — the pump electricity adds up. I'll irrigate twice if the sky stays dry: once right after planting to wake the seeds up, and once when the bolls are setting in August. If it rains, I skip it. The well is there, but I watch every yuan.

Weeds and bugs are the enemy. I'll spray herbicide once after the seedlings come up, and I'll keep an eye out for bollworms like I always do. If I see holes in the bolls, I spray insecticide. Last year wasn't too bad. I do the spraying myself with the backpack sprayer, though my back aches something fierce after.

I can't handle the heavy plow anymore, so I hired the Zhang boy to come through with his small tractor to turn the soil. The rest — planting, fertilizing, weeding, spraying, and all that picking — my family does. Picking cotton takes forever, little by little. We go out three or four times from September through October as the bolls open.

I expect about 250 jin of seed cotton per mu, maybe 280 if the weather is kind. That's what I usually get. I'm not trying to be the best in the village — I just need enough to buy my medicine, pay the electricity, and have some left for rice and oil.
